prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned prose that turns memory, the body and dream into an inner cosmos of rare imaginative scale

statement.case_for: My laureate is unchanged: Cărtărescu (B031). Only the citation wording changes. The case rests on the common literary criteria. His voice is recognizable. His formal ambition is sustained in long, architecturally ordered books, of which Blinding (the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid are the best-known public examples. Memory, the body and dream are worked into one metaphysical project, which gives the oeuvre imaginative and intellectual depth. The work spans decades and does not hang on a single book. In round 1 I asked whether Solenoid reorganizes the earlier preoccupations or only restates them. My colleagues' answers, and the chair's question, show that nobody here can settle this from the supplied record, and I cannot either. Public knowledge describes Solenoid as a different kind of book from the trilogy, a single long narrative with a different framing and a different relation to its material. That is mild support for development and not a finding. I am narrowing the citation to prose, with poetry as context. This is because poetry coverage in translation is the thinnest part of what I can evidence, and a citation should claim only what the committee can stand behind. I do not want the case to rest on a reading of Nobel's 'idealist' direction, nor on how widely it is shared. The six round-1 preferences coincide, but I treat that as correlated reasoning from shared public knowledge, not as an independent check on merit.
statement.case_against: The reservation is unchanged and still unresolved. The achievement is carried by dense, long-breathed Romanian prose whose syntax, rhythm and register I judge only through translation and public knowledge. Recurring imagery may be method, as Olsson suggests, or it may be repetition. The late digressive volumes may be uneven. I accept a standard of peaks and overall direction, but only if there are several peaks across more than one book and more than one decade. A single peak would not meet it. If expert reports or close reading showed that the later long fictions mostly restate the earlier ones, I would move to Tawada (B015). Her linguistic and formal invention across two languages is the most distinctive alternative on the shortlist. Adonis (B020) would be second, with the caveat that his prosody is also lost in translation. Tawada's case also depends on corpus coverage I cannot assess equally in Japanese and German. The move would therefore be a loss of confidence in the first choice, not a verdict that her achievement is greater.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg argues that a citation rewards an oeuvre's peaks and overall direction, not uniform quality, so unevenness in the late digressive volumes does not by itself weaken the case. He also says the citation should credit what survives translation (architecture, imaginative logic, sustained invention) and be modest about sentence-level music, and he keeps poetry secondary.
responses.response: I accept the peaks-and-direction standard with one condition: the peaks must be plural and spread across the career, or the standard would justify almost any writer with one great book. On that basis I think the Cărtărescu case can meet it, although I have not verified this by close reading. I also take his point about citation wording and have acted on it. My revised citation names the architecture, the imaginative scale and the inner-cosmos project, and says nothing about the music of the Romanian sentence. I part company with him on one thing. He says Tawada is harder to verify than Cărtărescu because wordplay is exposed to translation loss. I agree on the loss. But for us it argues for caution about her, not for a lower view of her achievement, and I would not let our access problem become a literary ranking.

responses.point: Palm's citation names prose and the specific works Blinding and Solenoid and leaves poetry out. She offers a provisional view that Solenoid changes the mode and widens the field of the earlier trilogy, and she says Michon's case would need the committee to state explicitly why a few books are enough.
responses.response: Her scoping is closest to where I have ended up. I now put prose at the centre and leave poetry out of the citation, because our access to the poetry is the least secure part of the record. I would not name individual titles in the citation itself. Titles can stay in the committee's reasoning, and a prize citation that lists books narrows the whole-oeuvre claim. I share her provisional reading of Solenoid and hold it with the same caveat that it is a judgement, not a finding. On Michon, I agree with her that the committee has not made the case that a few books suffice, and no member has argued it explicitly in round 1. Mattson's case is about concentration, and I accept that as a real kind of achievement. What it lacks, for now, is an argument that it has enough breadth and development to support a whole-oeuvre prize.

responses.point: Mattson says the main risk to Cărtărescu is that density and recurrence of imagery may be repetition. She wants the case argued from close reading of specific works, including Solenoid, and not from shared first-place rankings. She keeps Michon and Wright as serious alternatives for concentration of language and reinvention of narrative form.
responses.response: I agree that the committee should not count a shared first place as an answer to the repetition question, and my own file says the same. I would add one practical step: the committee should ask for readers' reports on Solenoid set against the Orbitor trilogy, and treat their conclusions as evidence we do not currently have. On her alternatives, I still see Michon's sentence-level achievement as real. But the case is built on language that translation reaches only partly, and the corpus is small. That leaves me with less to test for development than I have for Cărtărescu. Wright's formal ambition is evident, but I keep her literary achievement, which lies in polyphonic voice and structure, strictly apart from the importance of her subject. A few major novels leave open whether the body of work is mature. I do not think either of her alternatives is weak. They rest on a thinner evidential base than the one I am relying on.

responses.point: Olsson treats recurrence of imagery in a metaphysical project as partly the method, so the test is whether the later works change the architecture and not just the motifs. He says translation risk falls on sentence texture and less on the larger structure. He discloses that his scholarly work on the fragment, exile literature and Celan overlaps thematically with Adonis and Tawada.
responses.response: I agree that architecture, not motif, is the right test, and that is how I have framed my doubt. I would qualify one point. 'Recurrence is the method' cannot be accepted without evidence, because it could excuse any repetition. It needs a showing that the recurring images do different work in later books. I accept his claim that structure survives translation better than texture, but it is a claim and not a demonstrated fact, so I have kept the citation modest on style. On his disclosure, I read it as thematic context with no tie to a writer. It does mean that Adonis and Tawada, both among the alternatives I name, are also among his. The committee should read my alternatives and his as independent literary judgments and not as convergence that adds evidence. Those alternatives would only matter if the case for B031 weakened.

uncertainties: I have not independently verified sources or read the full corpus of any candidate. My judgements rest on public knowledge and translations.
Whether Solenoid reorganizes the preoccupations of the earlier trilogy or restates them is unresolved. My reading of it as a different mode is tentative and unverified by close reading.
Coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry and early work in translation is thin and uneven, which is why I have taken poetry out of the citation. The case therefore rests mainly on the major long fictions.

Translation limits differ by candidate, and comparing them is uneven. Romanian density, Japanese and German wordplay, Arabic prosody, Spanish verse and French syntax each lose different qualities. Expert reader reports, if the committee can obtain them, would help more than my inferences.
I cannot say how far the six aligned round-1 preferences reflect independent judgement and how far shared reliance on the same public knowledge. The convergence is not evidence of merit.
Whether a co-opted member votes in committee is undocumented. The six-vote structure with a four-vote majority and my simulated vote are modeling assumptions.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which shows no personal, institutional or professional tie to any shortlisted writer. My non-fiction practice, including my biography of Alfred Nobel and my work on influence campaigns and on Anna Maria Lenngren, is context. It is not evidence of a preference for any candidate, and my reading of Nobel's will rests on the idea that the case should stand on voice, form and depth. Olsson's disclosed thematic overlap with Adonis and Tawada is noted and not adjudicated. My voting status as a co-opted member is undocumented and is treated here as a modeling assumption.
